# Syllabus

<!-- GENERATED by build.mjs from content/*.md. Do not edit by hand. -->

11 modules · 100 lessons · 402 exercises · 35 projects. Each part is a few lessons followed by a project (🛠) that uses what those lessons taught.

Full lessons, exercises, project briefs and a progress tracker: **https://rgamz.github.io/fullstack_path/** (or open `index.html` locally).

## Modules

1. [Node.js](#1-nodejs) · 3–4 weeks
2. [Express.js](#2-expressjs) · 3 weeks
3. [Databases](#3-databases) · 3–4 weeks
4. [User Interface Design](#4-user-interface-design) · 1–2 weeks
5. [React.js Fundamentals](#5-reactjs-fundamentals) · 2–3 weeks (less if it's a refresher)
6. [Testing](#6-testing) · 2 weeks
7. [TypeScript](#7-typescript) · 2–3 weeks
8. [Advanced React](#8-advanced-react) · 3–4 weeks
9. [Next.js](#9-nextjs) · 3–4 weeks
10. [AI Engineering](#10-ai-engineering) · 3–4 weeks
11. [Launching Your Career](#11-launching-your-career) · Ongoing (start early!)

## 1. Node.js

*3–4 weeks.* JavaScript outside the browser. You'll write command-line tools, build an HTTP API using only Node's built-in modules, and finish with a small full-stack app, so that when you meet Express you know exactly what it does for you.

### Part 1: Getting started with Node

Install Node, learn how projects and modules are organised, and read and write files. You'll finish by building a to-do app that runs in your terminal.

- 1.1 What is Node.js? Setup and your first script *(1h)*
- 1.2 npm, package.json and modules *(1.5h)*
- 1.3 Reading and writing files with fs and path *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: CLI Task Manager**: A to-do app that runs in your terminal and saves tasks to a JSON file.

### Part 2: Build a Node API

Learn how the web talks (HTTP), then build a JSON API using nothing but Node's built-in http module: routing, path and query parameters, clean code structure and CORS. You'll finish with a travel destinations API a frontend can use.

- 1.4 The http module: your first server *(1h)*
- 1.5 HTTP and the request/response cycle *(1h)*
- 1.6 Routing and serving JSON *(1.5h)*
- 1.7 Path parameters and query parameters *(2h)*
- 1.8 Modularising your code *(1h)*
- 1.9 CORS *(45m)*
- 🛠 **Project: Destinations API (built-ins only)**: A JSON API of travel destinations, built with only Node's http module.

### Part 3: Build a full-stack Node app

Make one Node server deliver both a website and an API. You'll serve static files, accept data with POST requests, push live updates with Server-Sent Events and keep secrets in environment variables. The section ends with a live story board where new posts appear on everyone's screen.

- 1.10 Serving a website: static files *(1.5h)*
- 1.11 Handling POST requests and request bodies *(1.5h)*
- 1.12 Events, EventEmitter and Server-Sent Events *(1.5h)*
- 1.13 Environment variables and configuration *(45m)*
- 🛠 **Project: Live Story Board (full-stack)**: A website where people post short stories and everyone sees new ones appear live.

## 2. Express.js

*3 weeks.* In the Node module you built servers with the raw `http` module, parsing URLs, setting headers and reading bodies by hand. Express is a thin layer on top of that same server that does those chores for you, so you can spend your time on what your API actually does.

### Part 1: Build an Express API

Learn the building blocks of Express (routes, routers, middleware, error handling and validation) and how to design a clean REST API. You'll finish by building a Book Library API that you'll keep upgrading in later modules.

- 2.1 Hello Express *(1h)*
- 2.2 Routers and project structure *(1.5h)*
- 2.3 Middleware *(1.5h)*
- 2.4 REST API design and CRUD *(2h)*
- 2.5 Error handling *(1h)*
- 2.6 Validation *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Book Library REST API**: A complete in-memory CRUD API with routers, validation, central error handling, search and pagination.

### Part 2: Build a full-stack Express app

Serve a frontend from the same Express app, render HTML on the server with templates, and put your app online. You'll finish by building and deploying your own URL shortener.

- 2.7 Serving static files and templates *(1h)*
- 2.8 Deploying an Express app *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: URL Shortener**: Your own mini Bitly: shorten links, redirect visitors and count clicks, served from one Express app and deployed online.

### Part 3: Authentication and security

Let people create accounts and log in, keep each user's data private, and add the security defaults every public Express app needs. You'll finish by building a private journal app.

- 2.9 Authentication: passwords, sessions and JWT *(3h)*
- 2.10 Security essentials *(1h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Private Journal**: Users register, log in and keep journal entries that only they can see.

## 3. Databases

*3–4 weeks.* Store data properly. You'll learn SQL (the most valuable data skill you can have), design relational schemas, and connect your Express apps to SQLite and PostgreSQL, so your data survives restarts and many users can work with it safely at the same time.

### Part 1: Writing SQL queries

Learn what a database is and how to talk to one in SQL: reading, filtering, sorting, creating tables, changing data and summarising it. You'll finish with a SQL practice set that you keep on GitHub.

- 3.1 What is a database? *(1h)*
- 3.2 SQL basics: SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY *(2h)*
- 3.3 Creating tables and modifying data *(1.5h)*
- 3.4 Aggregation: COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: SQL practice set**: A GitHub repo of SQL you wrote yourself: your own dataset with questions, plus 15 solved practice problems.

### Part 2: Relationships and schema design

Real data is spread over many related tables. Learn to combine them with JOINs, design a clean schema from scratch, and keep it fast and correct with indexes and transactions. You'll finish by designing a complete online shop database, still in a SQL editor, with no app yet.

- 3.5 JOINs and relationships *(2h)*
- 3.6 Schema design and normalisation *(1.5h)*
- 3.7 Indexes and transactions *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Online shop database**: Design a complete shop database with keys, constraints, seed data, business queries, indexes and an order transaction.

### Part 3: Databases in your Node apps

Connect your Express apps to real databases: SQLite with Node's built-in module, then PostgreSQL with the pg package (hosted, and locally in Docker), safely protected against SQL injection. You'll also try an ORM with migrations and (optionally) MongoDB. You'll finish by upgrading your Book Library API and building a full-stack Expense Tracker.

- 3.8 Using SQLite from Node (and SQL injection) *(2h)*
- 3.9 PostgreSQL and hosted databases *(2h)*
- 3.10 Running Postgres locally with Docker *(1.5h)*
- 3.11 ORMs, query builders and migrations *(2h)*
- 3.12 (Optional) NoSQL with MongoDB *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Books API with a real database**: Upgrade your Express Book Library API from an in-memory array to PostgreSQL, with authors, tags, migrations and a seed script.
- 🛠 **Project: Expense Tracker**: A full-stack app to log what you spend, organise it in categories and see monthly reports and charts.

## 4. User Interface Design

*1–2 weeks.* You don't need to become a designer, but a handful of rules (hierarchy, type, colour, spacing and good states) make everything you build look and feel professional. Short module, big payoff for every project after it.

### Part 1: UI design fundamentals

The four tools designers use on every screen: hierarchy, typography, colour and spacing. Each lesson turns a principle into CSS you can reuse. You'll finish by designing and building a polished landing page for an imaginary product.

- 4.1 Visual hierarchy *(1h)*
- 4.2 Typography *(1h)*
- 4.3 Colour and accessibility *(1.5h)*
- 4.4 Spacing and layout *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Landing page**: A polished, responsive marketing page for an imaginary product, built with design tokens.

### Part 2: Figma and UX

Learn the design tool developers meet at work, and the UX side of interfaces: states, forms and feedback. You'll finish by redesigning one of your own old projects in Figma and then in code.

- 4.5 Figma basics *(1.5h)*
- 4.6 UX: states, forms and feedback *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Redesign an old project**: Redesign your least professional project in Figma, then rebuild its look in code with tokens and proper UI states.

## 5. React.js Fundamentals

*2–3 weeks (less if it's a refresher).* React is the most used library for building user interfaces. If you already learned React in the frontend part of your course, skim the theory, do the exercises quickly and spend your time on the projects, especially the last one, which connects React to your own Book Library API.

### Part 1: Static and data-driven pages

Set up a React project with Vite, split a page into components, pass data with props, and render lists and conditional content from an array. You'll finish by building and deploying a bookshelf page generated from a data file.

- 5.1 JSX and components *(1.5h)*
- 5.2 Props *(1.5h)*
- 5.3 Conditional rendering and lists *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Bookshelf page**: A responsive, data-driven page of your books built from components and a data.js array, deployed online.

### Part 2: State, events and forms

Make components interactive. You'll learn how state makes React re-render, how to handle events, update arrays and objects safely, and build forms the classic way and with React 19 form actions. You'll finish by building a memory card game with a start-screen form.

- 5.4 State and events *(2h)*
- 5.5 Forms *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Memory card game**: A card-matching game with a start-screen form, game state, move counter and a saved best score.

### Part 3: Side effects and APIs

Connect React to the world outside it: fetch data, run timers, debounce searches and deploy apps that talk to real APIs. You'll build a recipe finder on a public API, then a React frontend for the Book Library API you built in the Express and Databases modules.

- 5.6 Effects and data fetching *(2h)*
- 5.7 Build and deploy a React app *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Recipe Finder**: Search recipes from TheMealDB, view details and save favourites, with proper loading, empty and error states.
- 🛠 **Project: Books frontend**: A React frontend for your own Book Library API: list, search, add, edit, delete and toggle read.

## 6. Testing

*2 weeks.* Write code that proves your code works. You'll learn Vitest for unit tests and TDD, Supertest for your Books API, React Testing Library for components and Playwright for end-to-end tests, and make GitHub run all of them on every push.

### Part 1: Unit testing and TDD

What tests are for, how to write them with Vitest, how to work test-first, and how to replace things like the network or the clock with fakes. You'll finish by building a small utility library entirely test-first.

- 6.1 Why test? Types of tests *(45m)*
- 6.2 Vitest basics *(1.5h)*
- 6.3 Test-driven development (TDD) *(1.5h)*
- 6.4 Mocks, spies and fake timers *(1h)*
- 🛠 **Project: TDD utility library**: Build a small npm-style library (money, dates or strings) entirely test-first.

### Part 2: Testing APIs

Test your Express routes from the outside with Supertest, against a real test database, and make GitHub run your tests on every push. You'll finish by giving your Books API a complete test suite with CI.

- 6.5 Testing APIs with Supertest *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Fully tested Books API**: Give your Express + Postgres Books API a full test suite and run it on GitHub for every push.

### Part 3: Testing user interfaces

Test React components the way a user sees them with React Testing Library, then drive a real browser with Playwright. You'll finish by adding tests to the React apps you've already built.

- 6.6 Testing React components *(2h)*
- 6.7 End-to-end tests with Playwright *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Test your React apps**: Add React Testing Library tests to your Memory game and Recipe Finder, plus a Playwright test for your Books frontend, all running in CI.

## 7. TypeScript

*2–3 weeks.* JavaScript with types. TypeScript catches whole groups of bugs before you run your code and makes your editor much smarter, and most job listings expect it. You'll learn the language, then use it in a library, a React app and your Express API.

### Part 1: TypeScript fundamentals

Set up TypeScript and learn the type system step by step, from basic types to generics and utility types. You'll finish by converting your TDD utility library to strict TypeScript and publishing-ready type definitions.

- 7.1 Why TypeScript and setup *(1h)*
- 7.2 Basic types and inference *(1h)*
- 7.3 Object types: type aliases and interfaces *(1h)*
- 7.4 Unions, literal types and narrowing *(1.5h)*
- 7.5 Functions and generics *(1.5h)*
- 7.6 Utility types, keyof and typeof *(1h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Type-safe utility library**: Convert your TDD utility library to strict TypeScript, with exported types and .d.ts files.

### Part 2: TypeScript in React

Use TypeScript in a React project: typed props, state, events and generic components. You'll finish by building a typed Kanban board.

- 7.7 TypeScript with React *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Typed Kanban board**: A React + TypeScript task board with three columns, typed state and localStorage.

### Part 3: TypeScript and Express

Add types to a Node and Express backend, with Zod schemas as the single source of truth for request data. You'll finish by converting your Books API to TypeScript.

- 7.8 TypeScript with Node and Express *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Books API in TypeScript**: Convert your tested Express + Postgres Books API to strict TypeScript, without breaking a single test.

## 8. Advanced React

*3–4 weeks.* The patterns real React codebases use: composition, refs, context, reducers and custom hooks, then routing, server data with TanStack Query, code splitting, Tailwind and performance. You'll build a personal dashboard, an online shop front end, and finally take a deliberately slow app and make it fast.

### Part 1: Reusability and shared state

Learn how to build components that are easy to reuse, reach into the DOM with refs, share state without passing props through every level, organise complex updates with reducers, and package logic into your own hooks. You'll finish by building a personal dashboard full of widgets.

- 8.1 Composition and reusable components *(1.5h)*
- 8.2 Refs *(1h)*
- 8.3 Context *(1.5h)*
- 8.4 useReducer *(1.5h)*
- 8.5 Custom hooks *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Personal dashboard**: A start page with widgets (clock, todos, weather, GitHub, quote), built with reusable components, context, reducers and custom hooks.

### Part 2: Routing, data and styling

Turn a single page into a real multi-page app with React Router, load and cache server data with TanStack Query, split your code with lazy loading and catch errors with error boundaries, then style it all quickly with Tailwind. You'll finish by building the front end of an online shop.

- 8.6 React Router *(2h)*
- 8.7 Server state with TanStack Query *(2h)*
- 8.8 Suspense, lazy loading and error boundaries *(1.5h)*
- 8.9 Styling with Tailwind CSS *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Online shop (front end)**: A multi-page store with React Router, TanStack Query, a reducer-based cart, lazy routes, error boundaries and Tailwind.

### Part 3: Performance

Learn why React re-renders, how to measure it with the React DevTools Profiler, and which tools actually make a slow app fast. You'll finish by taking a deliberately slow 10,000-row product table and documenting how you sped it up.

- 8.10 Performance: re-renders, memo, deferred values and virtualisation *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Speed up a slow app**: Build a deliberately slow 10,000-row product table, measure it with the Profiler, fix it step by step and document before/after timings.

## 9. Next.js

*3–4 weeks.* Next.js is a React framework that puts routing, server rendering, database access and API endpoints in one project. This is where your frontend and backend skills merge, and you start building complete full-stack apps in a single codebase.

### Part 1: Build a Next.js app

Create a Next.js project, learn how folders become pages and layouts, understand which code runs on the server and which in the browser, and build dynamic pages with good metadata. You'll finish by building your own portfolio site.

- 9.1 What is Next.js? App Router basics *(1.5h)*
- 9.2 Layouts, navigation and styling *(1.5h)*
- 9.3 Server Components vs Client Components *(2h)*
- 9.4 Dynamic routes and metadata *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Portfolio site in Next.js**: Your own portfolio with project case studies from Markdown, dynamic pages and good metadata. You'll keep improving it until the Career module.

### Part 2: Making data flow

Load data on the server with proper loading and error states, change data with Server Actions, expose JSON with route handlers, and store everything in Postgres. You'll finish by building a bookmarks manager.

- 9.5 Data fetching, caching and streaming *(2h)*
- 9.6 Server Actions and forms *(2h)*
- 9.7 Route Handlers (API endpoints) *(1h)*
- 9.8 Databases in Next.js *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Bookmarks manager**: Save links with notes and tags in Postgres, filter by tag, edit and delete them, and expose them as a JSON API.

### Part 3: Authentication and shipping

Add sign-in so each user sees only their own data, protect pages and actions properly, and deploy to Vercel. You'll finish with two complete apps: a blog with an admin area, and a multi-user habit tracker.

- 9.9 Authentication *(2.5h)*
- 9.10 Deploying to Vercel *(1h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Full-stack blog / CMS**: A public blog plus a private admin area where you write, edit and publish posts. Postgres, Server Actions, auth and deployment in one project.
- 🛠 **Project: Habit tracker SaaS**: A multi-user app where people track daily habits and see streaks and charts. Every query is scoped to the signed-in user.

## 10. AI Engineering

*3–4 weeks.* Build real features on top of large language models: API calls, prompting, streaming, embeddings, RAG, tool use and agents. This module comes after the backend modules because every AI feature needs a server to keep API keys secret, and a database to remember things.

### Part 1: AI engineering fundamentals

Learn how LLMs work, call one from Node (hosted and local), write prompts that give reliable output, and stream answers to the browser. You'll finish by building your own ChatGPT-style chat app.

- 10.1 How LLMs work (for developers) *(1.5h)*
- 10.2 Calling an LLM API from Node *(2h)*
- 10.3 Open-source models, local models and free options *(1.5h)*
- 10.4 Prompt engineering *(2h)*
- 10.5 Streaming responses *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: AI chat app**: A ChatGPT-style app with your own assistant personality, streaming, history in Postgres and a daily limit.

### Part 2: Embeddings and RAG

Teach an LLM about your own documents. You'll learn embeddings and vector search with Postgres + pgvector, then retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and build a "chat with your docs" app with citations.

- 10.6 Embeddings and vector search *(2h)*
- 10.7 RAG: chat with your own data *(3h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Chat with your docs (RAG)**: Upload documents, ask questions in plain language, and get answers with citations, measured by an eval set.

### Part 3: Tools and agents

Let the model do things: call your functions, run in a loop as an agent, and connect to tools through MCP. Then learn to test, secure and budget AI features. You'll finish by building an agent that plans trips with real data.

- 10.8 Tool use / function calling *(2h)*
- 10.9 Agents and MCP *(2h)*
- 10.10 Evals, safety and cost *(1.5h)*
- 🛠 **Project: AI agent with tools**: A trip-planner agent that checks real weather, finds real places and saves a day-by-day itinerary, showing each step live.

## 11. Launching Your Career

*Ongoing (start early!).* Start this module in parallel from around the Express module, with an hour or two a week. A portfolio, a network and interview skills take months to build, so begin long before you feel "ready".

### Part 1: Portfolio and online presence

Make your work easy to find and easy to judge: three polished projects, a portfolio site, a strong GitHub profile, a one-page CV and an active LinkedIn. You'll finish with a job-ready checklist that says you can start applying.

- 11.1 Choose and polish 3 portfolio projects *(4h)*
- 11.2 Portfolio website and GitHub profile *(3h)*
- 11.3 CV / résumé *(2h)*
- 11.4 LinkedIn, networking and building in public *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Job-ready checklist**: Not code: everything in place so you can start applying with confidence.

### Part 2: Job search and interviews

Run your job search like a project, then prepare for the three kinds of interviews you'll meet: coding challenges, behavioural questions and take-home tasks. You'll finish with a six-week interview practice plan.

- 11.5 Job search strategy *(2h)*
- 11.6 Technical interviews: coding challenges *(ongoing)*
- 11.7 Behavioural interviews and take-home tasks *(2h)*
- 🛠 **Project: Interview practice plan**: A six-week plan: 30 coding problems with explanations, 6 STAR stories, 2 mock interviews and a timed take-home.

### Part 3: Capstone

Your signature project: your own idea, built for real users, combining everything from the whole curriculum. It becomes the centrepiece of your portfolio and your best source of interview stories.

- 🛠 **Project: Capstone project**: Your own idea solving a real problem for real people, built end to end with everything you've learned.
